newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey maintains offensive in Iraq despite protests.
newsitem.headline: Turkey maintains offensive in Iraq despite protests.

text.p: Turkey said on Tuesday its planes bombed Kurdish rebels fleeing northern Iraq into neighbouring countries as Middle Eastern nations increased protests at its two-week-old military incursion.

"Warplanes rained bombs today and yesterday on terrorists trying to escape from northern Iraq to Iran in the east and Syria in the west," Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency quoted military sources as saying.
The sources said troops had destroyed eight Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) camps as well as other shelters and stores used by the rebels in northern Iraq.

The anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress (INC) quoting satellite telephone links in the area, said on Tuesday that around 1,000 PKK fighters had crossed into Iraqi government controlled territory east of Kirkuk on Sunday.
The rebels were then escorted to Syria where they crossed the border at Sinjar, an INC spokesman told Reuters.
Meanwhile three bombs have exploded in the northern Iraqi capital of Arbil in the last three days, including one bomb heard all over the city on Tuesday morning, the INC said.
Arbil was the scene of fierce figting two weeks ago between the PKK and KDP forces trying to eject them from the city.

Turkey said that it had puts the PKK death toll in the offensive at around 1,750. Rebel sources say around 25 Turkish soldiers are being killed daily. A ban on reporters entering the region made confirmation impossible, but Western diplomats say they believe figures from both sides are exaggerated.

DEM news agency, which is close to the rebels, said in a statement that many village guard militiamen, enlisted to support Turkey's offensive, were refusing to fight and nearly 200 of them had returned to Turkey in the last week.
NATO-member Turkey's western allies and regional countries have expressed growing concern over the incursion into a Kurdish enclave protected by the West since the Gulf War ended in 1991.
Iranian president-elect Mohammad Khatami said on Tuesday Tehran had launched an official protest over the incursion and said it would not help settle differences.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz accused the United Nations Security Council of being "indifferent" to the Turkish incursion, the official Iraqi news agency said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has condemned the incursion and urged Ankara to pull out its troops.
Jordan urged Turkey to withdraw its troops from the region immediately to avoid a "dangerous escalation", the official Petra news agency quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying.
Turkish military officials said the offensive would continue until Turkey's Kurdish allies, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) of Massoud Barzani, had total control of northern Iraq.
"The operation will continue until Barzani says 'enough' and the KDP has attained complete authority in northern Iraq," a military source told Anatolian.
More than 10,000 Turkish troops streamed into northern Iraq two weeks ago to pursue PKK rebels who use the region as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
On Monday night, PKK guerrillas killed five villagers and wounded one in a raid on a village in the southeastern Turkish province of Diyarbakir, security officials told Reuters.
Turkey mounted a six-week, 35,000-man operation into the Kurdish-held northern Iraqi regions two years ago but failed to achieve its stated aim of clearing the area of PKK.
